title: The Lamb that was slain (Apocalypse 5)
hook: the Mass joins this heavenly liturgy (CCC 1090)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the door opened in heaven, and holy, holy, holy. Your line was they rest not. When did you remember the song that never stops? Day six hundred twenty-five.

Most people think Handel's Messiah ends with the Hallelujah chorus, because that's when audiences stand up. It doesn't. The Hallelujah comes at the end of the second part. The whole work closes later, with a slower, larger chorus, and then an Amen that goes on and on, voices climbing over each other for minutes. The words of that last chorus are worthy is the Lamb that was slain. Handel took them from the fifth chapter of the Apocalypse, where they are sung in heaven, by a choir far bigger than any concert hall could hold.
screen: `NOT THE HALLELUJAH.` → `THE LAST CHORUS OF MESSIAH.` → `WORTHY IS THE LAMB.`

segments.voice: Chapter five begins with a problem. In the right hand of the one on the throne is a scroll, written inside and out, sealed with seven seals. A strong angel calls out: who is worthy to open it? And no one in heaven or on earth or under the earth can. John starts to cry. He weeps much, he says. Then one of the elders tells him, weep not: the Lion of the tribe of Juda, the root of David, has won, and can open the scroll. So John turns to look for a lion. And what he sees is a Lamb. Standing, and yet looking as though it had been slain. You were told a lion; you see a lamb with its wounds still showing. That's the whole book in one image. The power that wins is a love that was killed and is alive. The Greek word John uses is arnion, which can mean a little lamb. The Lamb takes the scroll, and heaven erupts. The creatures and the elders fall down with harps and bowls of incense, which the text says are the prayers of the saints. Then thousands upon thousands of angels sing, in the Douay-Rheims: "The Lamb that was slain is worthy to receive power, and divinity, and wisdom, and strength, and honour, and glory, and benediction." Then every creature, in heaven, on earth, under the earth and in the sea, joins in. Catholics hear this at Mass. Just before Communion, the people sing to the Lamb of God three times, and the priest holds up the host and says, behold the Lamb of God. The Catechism says that in the liturgy on earth, the Church already shares in this heavenly one.
screen: `A SCROLL NO ONE CAN OPEN.` · `TOLD A LION, JOHN SEES A LAMB.` · `THE PRAYERS OF THE SAINTS.` · `THE LAMB OF GOD AT EVERY MASS.` · then, large: `THE LAMB THAT WAS SLAIN IS WORTHY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray the Agnus Dei, or sit with it. Settle, and breathe. Picture the scene: the throne, the scroll, the Lamb standing with its wounds showing, and every creature everywhere singing. Let your own small voice be one of them. If you pray, you can say the Agnus Dei slowly, the words the Church has sung for well over a thousand years, in your own language or in the old Latin: Agnus Dei, qui tollis peccata mundi, miserere nobis. Say it three times, once for each breath you need. If you don't pray, just picture the Lamb, and notice what it means that the winner has wounds. The bell holds the time.
The Lamb that was slain. Apocalypse five: the one worthy to open the scroll, a lamb with its wounds still showing, praised by every creature. Today's word.
screen: `THE LAMB THAT WAS SLAIN — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: worthy is the lamb. Today, the next time you're at Mass or hear the Lamb of God, remember the scroll and the song. Day six hundred twenty-five.

howItsDone: At every Mass, while the host is broken, the people sing or say the Agnus Dei, Lamb of God, three times, and the priest then shows the host with the words of John the Baptist, Behold the Lamb of God; the Church teaches that the earthly liturgy shares in the heavenly one.

fork.setup: you're John. no one in heaven or on earth can open the sealed scroll, and you're weeping. an elder says the Lion of Juda has won. you turn around. what do you see?
options: a lamb, standing, as though it had been slain.
fork.reveal: told a lion, John sees a lamb with its wounds still showing. the power that wins is a love that was killed and is alive.

original.note: Latin: Lamb of God, the chant sung before Communion at Mass, from John 1:29 and the Lamb of Apocalypse 5.

trapdoor: what you thought: a gentle, sentimental picture of Jesus.
what it means: the one who wins the world's history is a lamb that was killed and stands alive, and the Mass joins heaven's song to him.
what a scholar hears: arnion, 'little lamb', the Apocalypse's main title for Christ; announced as a lion, he appears as a lamb, 'standing as it were slain'.

sources.quoted: The Lamb that was slain is worthy to receive power, and divinity, and wisdom, and strength, and honour, and glory, and benediction.

notes: Messiah: the Hallelujah chorus ends Part II; the work closes with 'Worthy is the Lamb' and the Amen chorus. Confirm.
Arnion as a diminutive form ('little lamb'), though in Koine it often means simply 'lamb'. Script says 'can mean'. Confirm.
Agnus Dei in the Roman Mass since the late seventh century (Pope Sergius I): 'well over a thousand years'. Confirm.
CCC 1090 / Sacrosanctum Concilium 8: the earthly liturgy as a foretaste and sharing in the heavenly liturgy. Paraphrased.
Apocalypse 5:5 ('Weep not; behold the lion of the tribe of Juda…') paraphrased with Douay spelling 'Juda'.
